Team Name: Whispers from the Dust  

Looking for teammates!

Hi everyone!  

I’m building a storytelling project for the challenge Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA’s Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars.

​About Me
I’m passionate about space history, science communication, and turning real NASA hardware into stories that young people can feel and remember. I already have a clear project vision: an interactive experience where the abandoned equipment on the Moon and Mars
summary:
Abandoned but Not Forgotten is a NASA Hackathon 2026 project by Muhammad Mohsin Mehmood Sabir. It explores the human-made objects left behind on the Moon and Mars, treating them not simply as discarded equipment but as potential off-world heritage.   

The project shows how landing sites, spacecraft, rovers, scientific instruments, and even small personal or commemorative objects can remain preserved for decades because the Moon and Mars lack the weathering processes found on Earth. It presents these objects as evidence of humanity's early exploration beyond Earth. 

A major theme is why astronauts left equipment behind. Carrying everything back would require additional fuel and mass, so crews deliberately abandoned non-essential equipment to maximize scientific sample return. The project connects this engineering decision with the later historical and archaeological value of those objects. 

The project concludes with a question of preservation and ethics: as commercial and governmental missions increase, how can humanity continue exploring without damaging the historic sites and artifacts already on the Moon and Mars?
details:
1. Project title

Abandoned but Not Forgotten
Theme: Off-World Heritage · Field Survey
Created for: NASA's Hackathon 2026

2. Core idea

The project documents the material remains of space exploration and asks us to reconsider the word “abandoned.” Objects that were once disposable mission equipment may now represent historically important evidence of humanity's technological development.

3. Moon — human artifacts

The project highlights a census of lunar artifacts, including landers, rocket stages, rovers and golf balls. It emphasizes that lunar landing sites can remain remarkably preserved because there is no wind or rain to erase footprints and disturb objects.

Apollo 11 / Tranquility Base is presented as an important example. Its remaining artifacts include:

  • The Apollo 11 descent stage
  • The commemorative plaque
  • A gold olive branch
  • Apollo 1 mission patches
  • Medals honoring fallen American and Soviet spacefarers

4. Lunar Roving Vehicles

Apollo 15, 16 and 17 left their Lunar Roving Vehicles on the Moon after using them to travel away from their landing sites. The vehicles were positioned so they could record the ascent stage and then were powered down.

The project gives examples including:

  • Apollo 15: Hadley Rille, 27.8 km driven
  • Apollo 16: Descartes Highlands
  • Apollo 17: Taurus-Littrow Valley, including its famous patched fender made using taped maps

5. Surveyor missions

Before humans returned to the Moon, robotic Surveyor spacecraft helped establish that the lunar surface was suitable for landing. The project highlights Surveyor 1, Surveyor 3, and Surveyors 5–7.

Surveyor 3 is particularly interesting because astronauts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean later visited it during Apollo 12 and brought its camera back to Earth.

6. Why leave equipment behind?

This is one of the project's central engineering explanations.

The project argues that mass is extremely expensive to lift from another planetary body. Therefore, astronauts could leave non-essential equipment behind and use the saved mass for scientific samples. It describes Apollo crews as jettisoning more than 800 kg of non-essential equipment while returning 382 kg of lunar samples.

So the basic relationship is:

Less equipment returned → less ascent mass → more capacity for scientific samples.

7. Mars — a planetary archive

The project then shifts from the Moon to Mars, describing more than 190 artificial objects associated with exploration and estimating about 16.8 tons of material on the Martian surface.

These include:

  • Failed or crashed landers
  • Spent landers
  • Heat shields
  • Backshells
  • Sky cranes
  • Parachutes
  • Long-lived spacecraft such as Viking 1 and Viking 2

8. Rovers that went silent

The project also tells the stories of robotic explorers that exceeded their original expectations:

  • Spirit: Designed for 90 days but operated for about six years before becoming trapped in loose sand.
  • Opportunity: Operated for about 15 years and traveled 45 km before a global dust storm ended its mission.
  • Ingenuity: Completed 72 powered flights before rotor-tip damage ended its flying mission.

9. From space debris to heritage

Perhaps the most important conceptual part of the project is the question:

Trash or heritage?

The project argues that objects such as a urine bag, rover component, or commemorative olive branch can all become part of the same historical landscape. It presents Tranquility Base as an archaeological site comparable in significance to important ancient sites on Earth.

10. Protection and future exploration

The final section proposes thinking about these locations as protected heritage sites. It discusses:

  • Keep-Out Zones to prevent rocket exhaust from damaging fragile artifacts
  • Material science research using old spacecraft exposed to radiation and thermal cycling
  • Off-world ethics concerning how future commercial missions should interact with existing historic sites.

Overall project message

The strongest message of the project is:

The objects humans leave behind on other worlds are becoming part of humanity's history.

The project therefore connects space exploration + engineering + archaeology + heritage conservation + future space ethics. Its final image is especially powerful: the monuments of the space age are not necessarily large structures—they can be silent machines preserved in extraterrestrial dust.
